cases.candidate_question: Does T⊆V(I) imply vanishingIdeal(T)⊆I?
cases.mathematical_reason: The ideal inclusion is reversed: I⊆vanishingIdeal(T). Take R=Z, I=0 and T={(2)}. Then T⊆V(0), but vanishingIdeal(T)=(2) is not contained in 0.

cases.candidate_question: Is V(vanishingIdeal(T))=T for every subset T of Spec R?
cases.mathematical_reason: For R=Z and T={(0)}, the vanishing ideal is 0 and V(0)=Spec Z. The point (0) is not closed, and the required result is closure(T), not T itself.

cases.candidate_question: Is vanishingIdeal(V(I)) always I?
cases.mathematical_reason: Let R=k[t] and I=(t²). V(I)=V((t)), and its vanishing ideal is (t), strictly larger than (t²). The formula returns the radical.

cases.candidate_question: Can V(I+J) be written as V(I)∪V(J), and V(IJ) as V(I)∩V(J)?
cases.mathematical_reason: In Z take I=(2),J=(3). Their sum is Z with empty zero locus, whereas their product (6) has zero locus {(2),(3)}. V(I) and V(J) are disjoint nonempty singletons. The proposed operations give the wrong sets.

cases.candidate_question: Are all points of Spec R closed because the spectrum is T0?
cases.mathematical_reason: Spec Z is T0, but the prime (0) is not maximal and its closure is all of Spec Z. T0 does not imply T1 or Hausdorff, nor that every singleton is closed.

cases.candidate_question: Is the zero locus of every proper ideal irreducible?
cases.mathematical_reason: For R=k[x,y] and I=(xy), V(I)=V(x)∪V(y) with neither closed component containing the other. Its radical is not prime. Also V(R)=∅ is not irreducible under the nonempty convention.

cases.candidate_question: Does quasi-compactness of D(x) mean that D(x) contains only finitely many primes?
cases.mathematical_reason: Take R=Z and x=1. D(1)=Spec Z is quasi-compact but contains (0) and (p) for every rational prime p, hence infinitely many points. Quasi-compactness is the finite-subcover property, not finiteness of the set.

cases.candidate_question: If D(x) is empty, must x=0?
cases.mathematical_reason: In R=k[ε]/(ε²), the class ε is nonzero and nilpotent. It belongs to every prime ideal, so D(ε)=∅ despite ε≠0.

cases.candidate_question: Does D(x)⊆D(y) mean y belongs to the radical of (x)?
cases.mathematical_reason: Take a field k, x=0 and y=1. D(0)=∅⊆D(1)=Spec k, but 1 is not in √(0). The correct membership is x∈√(y).

cases.candidate_question: Is a ring element e with T=D(e) unique without requiring e²=e?
cases.mathematical_reason: In Q both e=1 and e=2 define D(e)=Spec Q, but they are distinct. Only 1 is idempotent; the uniqueness assertion is among idempotents.

cases.candidate_question: Does every unital commutative ring have a prime ideal, including the zero ring?
cases.mathematical_reason: The zero ring has 0=1 and only one ideal, the whole ring. Prime ideals must be proper, so its spectrum is empty. Nontriviality is essential.

cases.candidate_question: Does every ring homomorphism induce an injective map of spectra?
cases.mathematical_reason: For k→k[t], the distinct primes (0) and (t) of k[t] both contract to (0) in k. The induced map is continuous and obeys the zero-locus preimage formula, but is not injective.

cases.candidate_question: Does any injective ring homomorphism induce a closed embedding or closed map of spectra?
cases.mathematical_reason: The inclusion Z→Q induces the map from the one-point Spec Q to the generic point (0) of Spec Z. Its image is not closed. Injectivity of the ring map does not replace surjectivity in the closed-embedding theorem or integrality in the closed-map theorem.

cases.candidate_question: Is the image of Spec S→Spec R always exactly V(ker f)?
cases.mathematical_reason: For Z→Q the kernel is zero and V(0)=Spec Z, but the image consists only of (0). Its closure is V(0); the actual image need not be closed.

cases.candidate_question: Is every localization spectrum map an open embedding?
cases.mathematical_reason: Localize Z at all nonzero integers, obtaining Q. Its spectrum maps to {(0)}, which is not open in Spec Z: every basic neighborhood D(n) of (0), with n≠0, contains primes (p) not dividing n. The general result gives an embedding, whereas a single-element localization gives an open embedding.

cases.candidate_question: Is Spec R[1/x] identified with V(x), the primes containing x?
cases.mathematical_reason: For R=Z and x=2 the prime (2) is in V(2) but disappears after inverting 2. The image is D(2), the primes avoiding 2; in particular it contains (0).

cases.candidate_question: Does every quotient R/I have the same spectrum as R via the quotient map?
cases.mathematical_reason: For R=Z,I=(2), Spec(R/I) has one point whose image is (2), whereas Spec Z has many points. The hypothesis I⊆nilradical(R)=0 fails. Quotienting by a nil ideal, not an arbitrary ideal, preserves the whole spectrum.

cases.candidate_question: Does every integral ring homomorphism induce a surjection on spectra without injectivity?
cases.mathematical_reason: The quotient Z→Z/2Z is integral, but the only contracted prime is (2); the prime (3) of Z has no prime above it. Injectivity guarantees the needed absence of a kernel obstruction for all primes.

cases.candidate_question: Does going up hold for every injective homomorphism of domains?
cases.mathematical_reason: For Z→Q the prime J=(0) of Q contracts to (0)⊆(2), but Q has no prime contracting to (2). This extension is injective and both rings are domains, but it is not integral.

cases.candidate_question: Can two distinct comparable primes in S have the same contraction to R for an arbitrary R-algebra?
cases.mathematical_reason: For a field k and S=k[t], the primes (0)⊊(t) both contract to (0) in k. Integrality is what forbids this pair in the card.

cases.candidate_question: Is an ideal maximal exactly when its contraction is maximal, without primality or integrality hypotheses?
cases.mathematical_reason: Primality cannot be omitted: in the integral extension k→k[ε]/(ε²), I=0 contracts to the maximal ideal 0 of k, but I is not maximal. Integrality cannot be omitted either: for Z→Q the maximal ideal 0 contracts to the nonmaximal ideal 0 of Z.

cases.candidate_question: Does every proper ideal remain proper under an integral homomorphism, regardless of the kernel?
cases.mathematical_reason: Take f:k[t]→k evaluating at 0 and I=(t−1). The map is integral and I is proper, but f(t−1)=−1 is a unit, so the extension is all of k. I does not contain ker f=(t).

cases.candidate_question: May the integrality hypothesis be dropped from preservation of proper ideals containing the kernel?
cases.mathematical_reason: For Z→Q the kernel is zero, so (2) contains it, but the extension of (2) is Q because 2 is invertible. The map is not integral.

cases.candidate_question: Does any integral map from an integrally closed domain to a domain satisfy going down without injectivity or flatness?
cases.mathematical_reason: Let R=k[t],S=k and evaluate t at 0. Both rings are domains, R is integrally closed, and S is integral over R. For p=0⊊q=(t), the prime Q=0 of S lies over q. No prime of S contracts to p, so going down fails. The map is neither injective nor flat.

cases.candidate_question: Does an injective integral extension of an integrally closed domain satisfy this going-down theorem if S need not be a domain?
cases.mathematical_reason: Let R=k[t] and S=R×k, with r↦(r,r(0)). This map is injective and finite, hence integral, and R is normal. The prime Q=R×0 contracts to q=(t), and there is no prime strictly below Q: it is the generic and closed point of the separate Spec k component. Thus p=0⊊q has no prime below Q lying over p. S is not a domain.

cases.candidate_question: May integrally closedness of the base domain be dropped in integral-domain going down?
cases.mathematical_reason: Let S=Q[t,z] and R=Q[t²−1,t(t²−1),z]⊂S. S is integral over R since t satisfies X²−(t²−1)−1=0, and both are domains, but R is not integrally closed (t is not in R). Put Q=(t−1,z)⊂S, q=Q∩R, P₀=(t+1−z)⊂S and p=P₀∩R. Then p⊊q: evaluating at (−1,0) and (1,0) agrees on R, while z∉p and z∈q. Put a=t²−1; a∉p and S[1/a]=R[1/a], so P₀ is the unique prime over p. But P₀⊄Q since t+1−z has value 2 at (1,0). Thus no prime below Q lies over p.

cases.candidate_question: For a surjective ring map R→S, must dim R≤dim S?
cases.mathematical_reason: Evaluate k[t] at 0 to obtain the surjection k[t]→k. The source has dimension 1 and the target has dimension 0. The correct general inequality goes from the target dimension to the source dimension.

cases.candidate_question: Does adjoining an indeterminate leave the dimension of every Noetherian ring unchanged?
cases.mathematical_reason: A field k is Noetherian and has dimension 0, whereas k[t] has the strict prime chain (0)⊊(t) and dimension 1. The +1 in the polynomial dimension formula is essential.

cases.candidate_question: Is dim R_p always equal to dim R rather than to the height of p?
cases.mathematical_reason: Let R=k[x,y] and p=(x). The ring has dimension 2, while p has height 1 and R_p has dimension 1. Local dimension measures chains of primes below p, not all chains in R.
